title: Is public Wi-Fi safe? The FTC says usually
caption:
Is public Wi-Fi safe? The FTC says usually, thanks to encryption.
But scammers encrypt their fake sites too, so check the name.
Which one's the fake: left or right?

pinned_comment: Which one's the fake? LEFT: lumenbank.example or RIGHT: lumembank.example. Both are made up (.example addresses can never be real sites). Apple says some fake sites change "one or two letters of the website address," so this is the check to do before you log in. We'll reply with the answer in a few hours. LEFT or RIGHT?

pinned_backups.if: What's the answer? / LEFT or RIGHT guesses
pinned_backups.reply: RIGHT is the fake: lumembank.example, with an m where the real one, lumenbank.example, has an n. Both are made up for the video. That one letter is the whole trick; Apple's Safari guide says some fraudulent websites change "one or two letters of the website address."

pinned_backups.if: So I don't need a VPN?
pinned_backups.reply: The FTC article we used doesn't talk about VPNs, so the video makes no VPN claim either way. What it does say: "Because of the widespread use of encryption, connecting through a public Wi-Fi network is usually safe." Usually, not always, and a fake site is a risk on any network.

The FTC says connecting through public Wi-Fi "is usually safe" because most sites encrypt. The bigger risk it names is a fake site: "your data may be encrypted on its way to the site, but it won't be safe from scammers operating the site." So check the bank's address letter by letter, or use your bank's own app.

The FTC's 2023 article says to look for "a lock symbol or https in the address bar." Browsers have changed since: Chrome Help now calls the secure icon "Default (Secure)", and Safari shows the words "Not Secure" on unencrypted sites. And a scam site can be encrypted too, so the name check still matters.
Fair: the FTC article is dated February 2023, and we say so on screen. The Apple and Google pages we used for the name check were read on Nov 25, 2026, and both still say to check the site's address.

pinned_backups.if: Hackers can still see what I do on public Wi-Fi
pinned_backups.reply: The FTC's word is "usually" safe, not always. Its point is that "most websites do use encryption to protect your information." We didn't find a primary source with numbers on Wi-Fi attacks, so the video gives none.
The FTC article says: "It can be hard to tell if a mobile app uses encryption, but the majority do." The video sticks to websites, where you can check the address yourself.

youtube_description:
Is public Wi-Fi safe? The FTC's answer: usually, yes. Its consumer advice article "Are Public Wi-Fi Networks Safe? What You Need To Know" (February 2023) says: "In the early days of the internet, they often weren't secure. But things have changed."

Why? "That's because most websites didn't use encryption to scramble the data and protect it from hackers snooping on the network." Now: "Today, most websites do use encryption to protect your information." So the FTC says: "Because of the widespread use of encryption, connecting through a public Wi-Fi network is usually safe."

The catch: scammers "also create fake websites and encrypt them to make you think they're safe when they're not." And: "If you visit a scammer's website, your data may be encrypted on its way to the site, but it won't be safe from scammers operating the site." Encryption protects the trip, not the site.

So check the site's name, letter by letter. Apple's Safari guide: "Some fraudulent websites masquerade as trusted websites by changing one or two letters of the website address." Google's Chrome Help: "Even on secure sites, be careful with your personal information. To make sure you're on the correct site, check the site name in the address bar."

What about the lock? The FTC's 2023 article says: "Look for a lock symbol or https in the address bar to the left of the website address." Browsers have changed since: Google's Chrome Help now calls the secure-site icon "Default (Secure)", and Apple's Safari guide says the words "Not Secure" appear when a site isn't encrypted. Either way, a secure connection doesn't make a site honest, so the name check still matters.

One more from the FTC: "Create and use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication when it's available."

The test at the end: lumenbank.example and lumembank.example are both made up. Addresses ending in .example are reserved and can never be real websites. The answer comes in a reply under the pinned comment.

Fine print: The Wi-Fi list, the search bar, the FTC article card and the two address bars are re-created by hand from the sources' wording. The bank is fictional, the network name FREE_AIRPORT_WIFI is made up, and the phone, router, capsule and shops are our own paper drawings. Not affiliated with the FTC, Apple or Google.

- FTC Consumer Advice, "Are Public Wi-Fi Networks Safe? What You Need To Know" (February 2023), read Nov 25, 2026: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/are-public-wi-fi-networks-safe-what-you-need-know
